title: Audit a Default Before Letting It Decide for You
subtitle: Keep convenient defaults when they fit; change them when they do not.
description: For a setting, subscription, workflow, or template with meaningful consequences, identify the current default, compare the relevant alternatives, and make a deliberate keep-or-change decision with an easy rollback when possible.

lifeOsSource.hack: Review defaults that have meaningful cost, access, privacy, workflow, or compatibility consequences instead of changing settings merely because they are defaults.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pick one consequential default, identify what is currently selected, state what you need from the setting or service, compare only the realistic alternatives, note switching costs and important constraints, make a keep-or-change decision, and record how to reverse it when reversal matters.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What default did I inspect, what requirement mattered most, why did I keep or change it, and can I reverse the decision if the new choice is worse?

faq.question: Should I change every default setting?
faq.answer: No. A default can be perfectly suitable. Prioritize choices with meaningful consequences for money, access, privacy, workflow, compatibility, or recurring effort, and leave trivial defaults alone.

faq.question: What if I cannot tell which option is better?
faq.answer: Keep the current choice when the downside of changing is unclear, or make a reversible change and record the previous setting. Seek authoritative guidance when the option affects safety, legal obligations, account access, or another high-stakes area.

intro.html: A default is simply the option selected before you make an active choice. Sometimes that is exactly what you need. The useful habit is not to oppose defaults; it is to inspect the consequential ones and decide whether the selected option still fits your current requirements.

sections.title: 1. Pick a consequential default
sections.html: Choose a setting, subscription, workflow, template, permission, or account option that affects recurring cost, access, privacy, compatibility, or repeated work. Skip trivial choices whose consequences are too small to justify an audit.

sections.title: 2. State what you actually need
sections.html: Before comparing alternatives, write the requirement in plain language. For example: I need this notification only when action is required today, or I need this subscription while project X is active. This prevents the audit from becoming random preference switching.

sections.title: 3. Compare realistic alternatives
sections.html: Look only at options you could genuinely use. Note recurring cost, lost capability, extra steps, access implications, compatibility, and any condition that would make the alternative unsuitable. Use the provider's documentation for details that matter.

sections.title: 4. Keep, change, and record rollback
sections.html: Keep the default when it fits. Change it when another option clearly serves the requirement better and the switching cost is acceptable. When reversal matters, record the previous value or the steps needed to restore it, then revisit only if the new choice creates a real problem.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported uptake effects, invented attention savings and annualized impact, fabricated personal observations, arbitrary audit cadences, and overgeneralized privacy or security conclusions with a bounded default-choice review.
